            <p>All-sky photometric time-series missions have allowed for the monitoring of thousands of young (<i>t</i><sub>age</sub> < 800 Myr) stars in order to understand the evolution of stellar activity. Here, we developed a convolutional neural network (CNN), <span style="font-family: monospace">stella</span>, specifically trained to find flares in Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) short-cadence data. We applied the network to 3200 young stars in order to evaluate flare rates as a function of age and spectral type. The CNN takes a few seconds to identify flares on a single light curve. We also measured rotation periods for 1500 of our targets and find that flares of all amplitudes are present across all spot phases, suggesting high spot coverage across the entire surface. Additionally, flare rates and amplitudes decrease for stars <i>t</i><sub>age</sub> > 50 Myr across all temperatures <i>T</i><sub>eff</sub> ≥ 4000 K, while stars from 2300 ≤ <i>T</i><sub>eff</sub> < 4000 K show no evolution across 800 Myr. Stars of <i>T</i><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 4000 K also show higher flare rates and amplitudes across all ages. We investigate the effects of high flare rates on photoevaporative atmospheric mass loss for young planets. In the presence of flares, planets lose 4%–7% more atmosphere over the first 1 Gyr. <span style="font-family: monospace">stella</span> is an open-source Python toolkit hosted on GitHub and PyPI.</p>

        <!-- End info bottom --></div><!-- Start article full text --><div xmlns:book="http://api.iop.org/Book/1.0/" xmlns:c="http://ns.iop.org/namespaces/content" itemprop="articleBody" class="wd-jnl-art-full-text article-text"><h2 class="header-anchor" id="ajabac0as1" name="ajabac0as1"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left fa-icon--flip" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 320 512"><path d="M137.4 374.6c12.5 12.5 32.8 12.5 45.3 0l128-128c9.2-9.2 11.9-22.9 6.9-34.9s-16.6-19.8-29.6-19.8L32 192c-12.9 0-24.6 7.8-29.6 19.8s-2.2 25.7 6.9 34.9l128 128z"></path></svg>1. Introduction</h2><div class="article-text" data-mobile-collapse=""><p>Young stars are appealing targets for studying the early stages of stellar and exoplanet evolution. Stellar flares are energetic events caused by the reconnection of magnetic field lines, and there is evidence that they abound on very active coronal sources, such as pre-main-sequence stars (Benz & Güdel <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib10" id="fnref-ajabac0abib10">2010</a>). Flare rates are of particular interest due to their effects on the early stages of exoplanet evolution. They have been seen to cause phenomena such as increased photoevaporation of inner protoplanetary disks (Benz & Güdel <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib10" id="fnref-ajabac0abib10">2010</a>) and irreparable chemical changes to exoplanet atmospheres (Venot et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib102" id="fnref-ajabac0abib102">2016</a>). Flares can also expedite atmospheric erosion (Lammer et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib62" id="fnref-ajabac0abib62">2007</a>), particularly over the first few hundred million years, when the atmospheres of young planets are still contracting (Owen & Wu <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>).</p><p>The advent of high-precision time-series photometric missions, e.g., Kepler/K2 (Borucki et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib12" id="fnref-ajabac0abib12">2010</a>) and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS; Ricker et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib88" id="fnref-ajabac0abib88">2014</a>), have allowed for detailed studies of stellar activity across both spectral type and age (e.g., Davenport et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib22" id="fnref-ajabac0abib22">2014</a>; Hawley et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib47" id="fnref-ajabac0abib47">2014</a>). Using data from the 4 yr Kepler mission, Davenport (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib20" id="fnref-ajabac0abib20">2016</a>) identified ∼850,000 flares across 4000 stars spanning G0—M4 spectral types, and found a potential flare saturation limit as a function of Rossby number. It was later noted this sample may have significant pollution due to variable stars in this sample (Davenport et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib21" id="fnref-ajabac0abib21">2019</a>). More recently, Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>) conducted a flare search of all two-minute cadence stars observed in Sectors 1 and 2 of TESS. Of the entire sample, they found 1228 flaring stars with a total of ∼8700 flares, with the most flares occurring on >M4.5 dwarfs.</p><p>Stars are known to spin down as they age (Soderblom <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib95" id="fnref-ajabac0abib95">2010</a>). The generation of magnetic fields is driven by the conversion of kinetic to magnetic energy through dynamo theory. Notsu et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib76" id="fnref-ajabac0abib76">2013</a>) and Candelaresi et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib14" id="fnref-ajabac0abib14">2014</a>) found flare rates decrease with rotation period, a proxy for age (Noyes et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib77" id="fnref-ajabac0abib77">1984</a>), and flare energy. Additionally, Notsu et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib76" id="fnref-ajabac0abib76">2013</a>) found that the magnetic energy released by superflares identified in Kepler data can be explained by the magnetic energy stored near starspots, concentrated regions of magnetic field lines (Dun et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib32" id="fnref-ajabac0abib32">2007</a>). More recently, Ilin et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib53" id="fnref-ajabac0abib53">2019</a>) identified and analyzed K2 data for the Pleiades, Praesepe, and M67, and found a decrease in flaring activity with an increase in age. There was a sharper decrease in activity for stars with higher effective temperatures, <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub>.</p><p>Using short-cadence K2 light curves, Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib31" id="fnref-ajabac0abib31">2018</a>) explored the relation between starspots and flares. The identified flares appeared to show no correlation with the phase of the spot grouping, i.e., the spottier hemisphere and the less spotty hemisphere both had similar flare counts. Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib31" id="fnref-ajabac0abib31">2018</a>) also noticed that faster rotators showed greater flaring activity. Repeating similar studies, Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib30" id="fnref-ajabac0abib30">2019</a>) looked at 167 M dwarfs and Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib29" id="fnref-ajabac0abib29">2020</a>) looked at 158 G-M main-sequence stars in TESS short-cadence light curves observed in Sectors 1–13. Again, they found no correlation between the spot phase and flares at any energy.</p><p>Roettenbacher & Vida (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib90" id="fnref-ajabac0abib90">2018</a>) conducted a similar study with a sample of 119 main-sequence stars observed during the Kepler mission. Within this sample of stars, Roettenbacher & Vida (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib90" id="fnref-ajabac0abib90">2018</a>) found that low-amplitude flares are correlated with spot groupings. However, the superflares followed similar trends and were detected across all spot phases. Detailed studies of the Sun have revealed that low-amplitude flares are associated with the presence of sunspots (Zhang et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib106" id="fnref-ajabac0abib106">2008</a>). While Roettenbacher & Vida (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib90" id="fnref-ajabac0abib90">2018</a>) found similar trends to that of the Sun, Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib31" id="fnref-ajabac0abib31">2018</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib30" id="fnref-ajabac0abib30">2019</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib29" id="fnref-ajabac0abib29">2020</a>) did not.</p><p>The previously discussed flare detection studies relied on detrending a light curve and using outlier detection heuristics for identifying flare events. Most detection algorithms apply statistical criteria similar to those defined in Chang et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib16" id="fnref-ajabac0abib16">2015</a>) on a detrended light curve. The criteria defined in Chang et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib16" id="fnref-ajabac0abib16">2015</a>) predominantly rely on at least three consecutive cadences that lie ≥3<em>σ</em> above the median of the light curve. Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>) relied on fitting a spline to the underlying stellar variability and identifying flare candidates as at least six minutes (three cadences) of flux 3<em>σ</em> above the detrended light-curve flux. Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib31" id="fnref-ajabac0abib31">2018</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib30" id="fnref-ajabac0abib30">2019</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib29" id="fnref-ajabac0abib29">2020</a>) removed the underlying spot modulation and marked at least two consecutive cadences ≥2.5<em>σ</em> above the median light curve as potential flares. Roettenbacher & Vida (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib90" id="fnref-ajabac0abib90">2018</a>) used a RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) algorithm, which identifies and subtracts inliers (the underlying light curve) before searching for outliers above a given detection limit (Vida & Roettenbacher <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib104" id="fnref-ajabac0abib104">2018</a>). The outliers are flagged as flare candidates.</p><p>However, light-curve detrending has the potential to remove low-energy flares because aggressive spot variability models can include cadences that may belong to these flares. In turn, this could bias flare detection toward the highest-energy flares and affect modeled flare energies. For example, Davenport et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib22" id="fnref-ajabac0abib22">2014</a>) do not find flares below ∼10<sup>33</sup> ergs across a range of spectral types. This is additionally true for having a set outlier cut, where low-energy flares may not lie above this threshold. Because individual flares are believed to originate from the same physical processes, they exhibit similar time evolution (Benz & Güdel <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib10" id="fnref-ajabac0abib10">2010</a>) and therefore similar characteristic shapes in photometric data. Although at some point there will be a noise level to the flare amplitudes we are able to detect, this proves promising for using machine-learning algorithms to identify such a feature.</p><p>Machine-learning algorithms comprise a set of techniques in which models are derived primarily from the data presented to them. Generically, the key informative or distinguishing features of these data must also be presented to the algorithms. However, in a subset of techniques, deep learning algorithms can be presented with raw data, and the models themselves identify the critical informative features.</p><p>Several instances of machine learning have already been applied to time series data for planetary and stellar studies. Shallue & Vanderburg (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib94" id="fnref-ajabac0abib94">2018</a>) trained CNNs to identify exoplanet transits and present discoveries of new planet candidates. Ansdell et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib4" id="fnref-ajabac0abib4">2018</a>) expanded upon these techniques by including centroid positions of the stars to train their CNN. All three methods relied on detrended light curves and hand-labeled transit events. Pearson et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib82" id="fnref-ajabac0abib82">2018</a>) also used CNNs to search for new exoplanet candidates and trained their network on simulated data with underlying stellar variability. They trained on light curves with underlying photometric variability.</p><p>As young stars are more rapidly rotating than main-sequence stars, it may be expected that these stars exhibit higher flare rates. Due to the high magnetic activity and spot coverage of rapidly rotating stars (Montet et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib69" id="fnref-ajabac0abib69">2017</a>; Morris <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib70" id="fnref-ajabac0abib70">2020</a>), pre-main sequence (PMS) and young (<em>t</em><sub>age</sub> < 800 Myr) stars may prove to be excellent targets for understanding the relationship between starspots and flares. Here, we present the results of a CNN trained to identify flares in short-cadence TESS data as applied to young stars observed in Sectors 1-20 of TESS. The CNN is part of the new open-source software package, <tt>stella</tt> (Feinstein et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib110" id="fnref-ajabac0abib110">2020</a>).<sup class="fnref"><a class="fnref" href="#ajabac0afn1">
               11
            </a></sup>
             Our analysis is aimed to better understand flare statistics down to low energies, how they relate to spot groupings, and general trends in flare rates with respect to age and spectral type.</p><p>The paper is presented as follows: Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as2">2</a> will discuss the details of creating and validating the CNN. Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as3">3</a> will describe the young stellar sample, rotation period measurements, and flare identification used in this work. Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as4">4</a> will present our analysis of the newly identified flares with relation to spots, and Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as5">5</a> will provide a discussion of these results and their implications for exoplanets. We will conclude in Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as6">6</a>.</p></div><h2 class="header-anchor" id="ajabac0as2" name="ajabac0as2"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left fa-icon--flip" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 320 512"><path d="M137.4 374.6c12.5 12.5 32.8 12.5 45.3 0l128-128c9.2-9.2 11.9-22.9 6.9-34.9s-16.6-19.8-29.6-19.8L32 192c-12.9 0-24.6 7.8-29.6 19.8s-2.2 25.7 6.9 34.9l128 128z"></path></svg>2. The Convolutional Neural Network: <tt>stella</tt>
         </h2><div class="article-text" data-mobile-collapse=""><p>Neural networks learn features from a training data set that consists of input examples with corresponding classifying labels. When presented with samples labeled by a given class, supervised learning techniques are used to optimize the network weights such that they collectively identify sets of features relevant for those classes. Neural networks are often referred to as “deep learning” because they consist of a series of hierarchical computational layers, where each layer is made up of a series of neurons, or scalar valued units (Aggarwal <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib2" id="fnref-ajabac0abib2">2015</a>). The input to a neuron is calculated by weighting the outputs from neurons in the previous layer, then adding a bias term and applying a nonlinear activation function (Rosenblatt <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib91" id="fnref-ajabac0abib91">1962</a>). The activation function is a key component of a neural network, because it enables the network to solve nonlinear problems. For classification problems (such as used in this work), the final output of a neural network is normalized to a value between 0 and 1, which represents a ranking (but not necessarily a probability; see Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as2-5">2.5</a>) of the input example belonging to the positive class (in our case, flares).</p><p>Fully connected neural networks are not designed to explicitly account for spatial structure in data. Neurons in a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), in contrast, are only connected to local regions in the preceding layer, allowing them to detect local features in the data. CNNs are promising for astronomical purposes, as they can be optimized for computer vision tasks. This means the algorithms can identify patterns and features within complex data sets without requiring prior information on said features. Stellar flares exhibit characteristic shapes in time and flux space, and therefore training a CNN to identify this specific feature is promising. In CNNs, a convolution layer applies filters to the data, resulting in feature maps from each layer (LeCun et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib63" id="fnref-ajabac0abib63">2015</a>). The weights in a given filter increase when they see certain types of features in the data that they have been optimized for, and this information is then fed into the next layer. The number of feature maps, as well as the complexity of the detected features, typically increases with network depth. Pooling layers aggregate values within small neighborhoods (strides) of neurons along the input by calculating and outputting a summary statistic (e.g., mean, median, max) (Krizhevsky et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib61" id="fnref-ajabac0abib61">2012</a>). Pooling is primarily used to reduce the number of input pixels to the next layer. This allows the feature maps in the next convolutional layer to have a wider view of the input but at lower resolution and without increasing the number of trainable parameters.</p><p>Neural networks are useful for scientific research for several reasons. First, they can in many cases outperform physically parameterized modeling or human inspection techniques in their prediction accuracy: this is attributed to their flexibility in identifying critical data representations that are indicative of important aspects of the data with which they are presented. Moreover, unlike human vetting, deep learning models are systematic, which is important for calculating metrics like occurrence rates. Neural networks are also typically fast in the inference stage: once models are trained, it can take just seconds to apply to hundreds of thousands of new examples; similarly, they are sometimes upgradeable, such that improved models can be quickly retrained and applied to new data. However, networks can suffer from challenges with bias and uncertainty quantification. The data sets used to train a network contain biases, which the network is optimized to represent. Additionally, there are an increasing number of methods for quantifying errors in networks, but it is an area of active study to provide accurate and interpretable error estimates.</p><h3 id="ajabac0as2-1" name="ajabac0as2-1">2.1. Data Preparation: Training, Validation, and Test Sets</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The TESS targets used in training, validating, and testing the CNN are taken from Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>), who searched for flares in the first two sectors of the TESS mission. The light curves consist of integrated flux measurements taken at a two-minute cadence over roughly 27 days; they were made publicly available with the first TESS data releases through the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). Similarly to Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>), we split each light curve into individual orbits, and normalized the Simple Aperture Photometry flux (SAP flux) separately for each orbit.</p><p>For supervised learning tasks, neural networks require input data that are uniformly sampled to train properly. For the inputs to the CNN implemented here, we used a data set of one-dimensional time series where all elements have the same number of two-minute cadences. We found that a length of 200 cadences provided enough information about the baseline flux surrounding a given flare. Longer baselines often predicted high probabilities for both rotational signatures and flares instead of just flares. This baseline also provided ample flare and non-flare sets to train, validate, and test on. Following the methods of Pearson et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib82" id="fnref-ajabac0abib82">2018</a>), we ensured all known flare peak times from the Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>) catalog were centered at the 100th cadence (i.e., centered). Each of these light-curve snippets are hereafter referred to as a “sample.” All of the steps (e.g., training and ensembling a series of CNN models) discussed in this section are incorporated into the open-source Python package <tt>stella</tt>.<sup class="fnref"><a class="fnref" href="#ajabac0afn1">
                  11
               </a></sup> 
               <tt>stella</tt> and the CNN architecture described here are specifically tailored for finding flares in TESS short-cadence light curves, and they should not be applied to other photometric time-series data.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as2-2" name="ajabac0as2-2">2.2. Labels</h3><div class="article-text"><p>We used a binary labeling scheme of “flare” and “non-flare” for the samples (see Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af1">1</a> for examples of the samples). For the flare examples, we used the peak times of flares identified by Günther et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib45" id="fnref-ajabac0abib45">2020</a>). Non-flare samples were centered on locations in the light curves at least 100 cadences from a flare. Our final training set contains 5389 hand-labeled flare examples and created 17,684 non-flare examples for a 30% positive class data set. We then randomly divided the data set into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets. We used the validation set to tune the network and train hyperparameters, and then used the test set to evaluate the final model performance (Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as2-4">2.4</a>).</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af1" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af1" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af1_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 1."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 1. First, not all flares, particularly those at low energy, were identified in the original catalog, and therefore some have a “non-flare” label in the training set (Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af4">4</a>; false negatives). Second, we found the catalog is off in peak flare time for some cases, and therefore some flares have been classified as false positives when evaluating the validation set. This is because those flares were not at the center cadence of the example.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as2-3" name="ajabac0as2-3">2.3. Network Architecture and Training</h3><div class="article-text"><p>Our CNN architecture, shown in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af2">2</a>, is implemented in <tt>tf.keras</tt>, which is TensorFlow’s (Abadi et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib1" id="fnref-ajabac0abib1">2016</a>) open-source, high-level implementation of the Keras API specification (Chollet et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib17" id="fnref-ajabac0abib17">2018</a>). The network consists of a one-dimensional convolutional column with global max pooling and dropout, the results of which are flattened and fed into a series of fully connected (or “dense”) layers ending in a sigmoid function that produces an output in the range [0, 1]. This output loosely represents the “score” of how likely a given example is to be a flare (1) or non-flare (0) event.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af2" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af2" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af2_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 2."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 2. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>The usage of global max pooling and dropout are standard practices with state-of-the-art CNNs (e.g., ImageNet; He et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib49" id="fnref-ajabac0abib49">2016</a>) to improve model performance. Max pooling downsamples the feature maps in a given layer by “pooling” (taking the maximum of) the output neurons within a given region, which can reduce the number of model parameters while increasing generalization (e.g., Lin et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib64" id="fnref-ajabac0abib64">2013</a>). Dropout helps prevent model overfitting by randomly “dropping” (or setting to zero) some fraction of the output neurons in a given layer during training to prevent the model from becoming overly dependent on any of its features (Srivastava et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib96" id="fnref-ajabac0abib96">2014</a>).</p><p>Training neural networks involves inputting samples and then minimizing a cost function that measures how far off the network’s predictions are from the truth. This is done through backpropagation, which updates the model parameters to reduce the value of the cost function. For model training, we used the Adam optimization algorithm (Kingma & Ba <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib58" id="fnref-ajabac0abib58">2014</a>) to minimize the binary cross-entropy error function. The Adam optimizer was run with a learning rate of <em>α</em> = 10<sup>−3</sup> (this controls the degree to which the weights are updated with each iteration), exponential decay rates of <em>β</em> = 0.9 and <em>β</em> = 0.999 (for the first and second moment estimates), and <em><img src="https://cdn.images.iop.org/Entities/epsi.gif" alt="epsilon" align="baseline" /></em> = 10<sup>−8</sup> (a small number to prevent any division by zero in the implementation).</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as2-4" name="ajabac0as2-4">2.4. Model Evaluation</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The exact model architecture, kernel sizes, etc., were chosen based on a trial and error approach to avoid overfitting the model. Overfitting was evaluated using four standard machine-learning metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and average precision. Accuracy is the fraction of correct classifications by the model for both classes (flares and non-flares) at a given threshold for deciding when the model output becomes a positive class; we use a threshold of 0.5 for our accuracy calculations and overall analysis. Precision is the fraction of flares classified as flares that are true flares, while recall is the fraction of true flares recovered by the model. The average precision summarizes the precision–recall curve as the weighted mean of precisions achieved at each threshold, i.e., it is the area under the precision–recall curve evaluated across various threshold values, not just 0.5, as the precision is.</p><p>We use model ensembling to produce a distribution of 10 independently trained versions of the same model with different random parameter initializations. We then average the predictions across the 10 models and evaluate the abovementioned metrics to establish more robust classifications. Diagnostic plots for the performance of the 10 <tt>stella</tt> models are shown in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af3">3</a>. The left column demonstrates the evolution of the accuracy (top) and loss (bottom) functions for both the training and validation sets. As the accuracy converges toward 1 and the loss toward 0, we note that the models are not being overfitted to the data. The receiver operating characteristics (ROC; top right) visualizes the trade-off of true- and false-positive rates identified in the validation and test sets. The ROC is summarized by the area under the curve (AUC), where an AUC ∼ 1 reveals the classification was successful. We obtain an AUC of 0.997 ± 0.002 and 0.993 ± 0.002 for the validation and test sets, respectively. The precision–recall curves for the validation and test sets are shown in the bottom right of Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af3">3</a>.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af3" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af3" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af3_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 3."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 3. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure></div><h3 id="ajabac0as2-5" name="ajabac0as2-5">2.5. Determining Probabilities of Events</h3><div class="article-text"><p>In general, the output of a neural network classifier is not a probability (Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib74" id="fnref-ajabac0abib74">2005</a>), but rather a ranking or score of a given example being associated with the positive class (in our case, a true flare). In some cases, however, the network output may happen to be calibrated such that it is a good estimate of the probability. To test whether this is the case, we calculated the fraction of models across our ensemble that return the flare classification (assuming a threshold of 0.5) for each example in the test set. We then made a histogram of these values with bins spaced such that each bin contains the same number of targets. For each bin, we then calculated the fraction of true flares using the known labels and compared this value to the fraction of flare classifications by the model: if the model output happens to be calibrated, then these two values should match in each bin. The results are shown in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af6">6</a>, which illustrates a monotonically increasing function near the one-to-one line, indicating that the model is indeed fairly well-calibrated and we can use our model output as a rough estimate of probability. We note that there is no measure of uncertainty associated with each classification.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af6" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af6" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af6_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 6."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 6. Young stars are known to be more active than main-sequence stars. Tracing the evolution of flaring activity can provide insight into the first few hundred million years of a star or planet’s life.</p><h3 id="ajabac0as3-1" name="ajabac0as3-1">3.1. Selecting the Young Stellar Population</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The young stars selected for this sample are high-confidence (> 50%) members of nearby young moving groups, young open clusters, OB associations, and star-forming regions (see Table <a class="tabref" href="#ajabac0at1">1</a>). Each of these stellar populations are comprised of coeval stars with common kinematics spanning a broad range of masses (Zuckerman et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib109" id="fnref-ajabac0abib109">2004</a>). The ages of the stellar populations evaluated in this study range from ∼1–800 Myr. Thus, they are powerful tools for understanding stellar properties as a function of age, and sample key early times in the formation and evolution of stars and planets.</p><div tabindex="-1" id="ajabac0at1" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only"><p><b id="ajabac0at1-label">Table 1.</b> Number of Stars from Each Young Stellar Population</p><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0at1" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0at1_lr.gif" data-toolbar-type="table" data-toolbar-title="Table 1"><colgroup><col align="left"></col><col align="left"></col><col align="left"></col><col align="left"></col></colgroup><thead><tr valign="top"><th scope="col" colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="left">Population</th><th scope="col" colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="center">Age (Myr)</th><th scope="col" colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="center">Count</th><th scope="col" colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="left">Age Ref.</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr valign="top"><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="left">AB Doradus</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" align="center">

			Download table as: 
            <span class="btn-multi-block"><a class="btn btn-primary wd-jnl-art-btn-ascii" id="wd-jnl-art-btn-ascii-ajabac0at1" aria-labelledby="wd-jnl-art-btn-ascii-ajabac0at1 ajabac0at1-label" href="/1538-3881/160/5/219/suppdata/ajabac0at1_ascii.txt?doi=10.3847/1538-3881/abac0a" target="_blank">ASCII</a><a class="btn btn-primary wd-jnl-art-btn-typeset typeset-table-img" href="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0at1_lr.gif" id="wd-jnl-art-btn-typeset-ajabac0at1" aria-labelledby="wd-jnl-art-btn-typeset-ajabac0at1 ajabac0at1-label" target="_blank">Typeset image</a></span></p></div><p>After compiling a list of candidate young stars by aggregating selected <em>TESS</em> Guest Investigator proposals and data from Faherty et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib33" id="fnref-ajabac0abib33">2018</a>), we used <tt>astroquery</tt> to access Gaia DR2 to retrieve proper motions, parallaxes, and radial velocities (when available) for the stars (Gaia Collaboration et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib39" id="fnref-ajabac0abib39">2016</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib38" id="fnref-ajabac0abib38">2018</a>). We used derived effective temperatures, <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub>, for the stars from the TESS Input Catalog (TIC) V8. We used <tt>BANYAN-</tt>Σ<sup class="fnref"><a class="fnref" href="#ajabac0afn2">
                  12
               </a></sup>
                to reconfirm and assign population memberships (Gagné et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib37" id="fnref-ajabac0abib37">2018</a>). Using the stars’ kinematics, <tt>BANYAN-</tt>Σ derives a Bayesian probability of membership to 27 known coeval populations. We include stars with membership probabilities ≥50%, which yields a sample of 3193 stars observed at two-minute cadence observed in Sectors 1–20 (Table <a class="tabref" href="#ajabac0at1">1</a>). In this sample, 2345 of the stars were observed in a single sector, 609 in two sectors, 103 in ≥3 sectors, and 7 in 13 sectors (the continuous viewing zone) of TESS data.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as3-2" name="ajabac0as3-2">3.2. TESS Light-curve Preprocessing</h3><div class="article-text"><p>We used <tt>lightkurve</tt>
               <sup class="fnref"><a class="fnref" href="#ajabac0afn3">
                  13
               </a></sup>
                to download the target pixel files (TPFs) for all stars in our sample. In general, the Science Processing Operations Center (SPOC) preprocessed light curves were used with the pipeline default aperture. However, we found the pipeline was returning higher than expected scatter or negative flux-value light curves for several faint <em>T</em><sub>mag</sub> > 14 stars. Specifically, we found the background model generated was overcorrecting for some sources (seen in two examples in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af7">7</a>) where the baseline background flux is not centered around zero.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af7" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af7" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af7_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 7."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 7. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>To mitigate this issue, and for consistency, we completed our own light-curve background subtraction and aperture photometry. We follow the 1D background estimation in Feinstein et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib35" id="fnref-ajabac0abib35">2019a</a>), subtract this background model from the two-minute TPFs, and extract photometry using the SPOC identified aperture for all sources.</p><p>In addition, we use the pipeline-assigned quality flags to mask bad regions in the light curve. We use cadences with quality flags 0 and 512. Upon visual inspection, we found that quality flag 512 (“impulsive outlier removed before cotrending”) at times removes the peak of flares across a range of amplitudes. To mitigate potential biases while calculating flare energies, we included this quality flag in the catalog. We additionally removed the first 200 cadences of each orbit, to minimize earthshine contamination.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as3-3" name="ajabac0as3-3">3.3. Measuring Rotation Periods</h3><div class="article-text"><p>One of the primary goals of this work is study the correlation of flare events and starspots. The rotation period (<em>P</em><sub>rot</sub>) of a star can be measured through photometric spot variability. Thus, we created a subsample of stars with measurable rotation periods in order to explore the relationship between flares and spots. Rotation periods for stars observed in multiple sectors were identified per sector. We limited measured periods to <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub> <12 days; we found the contamination from earthshine at the end of each orbit resulted in a strong periodic signal. Young stars are known to have short rotation periods, on the order of a few days, so this additional upper limit does not dramatically bias our sample (Barnes <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib6" id="fnref-ajabac0abib6">2003</a>). Statistics of the stars in our entire sample can be seen in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af8">8</a> and Table <a class="tabref" href="#ajabac0at1">1</a>.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af8" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af8" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af8_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 8."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 8. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>We used a Lomb-Scargle periodogram implemented in <tt>astropy</tt> to identify rotational signatures (Lomb <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib65" id="fnref-ajabac0abib65">1976</a>; Scargle <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib92" id="fnref-ajabac0abib92">1982</a>). We defined a set of criteria for the periodogram to pass in order to remove weak or nonexistent rotation periods, highly unlikely rotation periods, or light curves that are dominated by noise or data gaps. The criteria as as follows: (A) the period must be less than 12 days; (B) the width of a Gaussian fit to the peak power must be less than 40% of the peak period; (C) the secondary peak in the power spectrum must be 4% weaker than the primary peak. Letters above correspond to a row in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af9">9</a> as examples for each criterion: each one reduces the possibility of catching a light curve that does not have a rotation period.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af9" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af9" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af9_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 9."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 9. (A) TIC 3837491. There was no period measured for this light curve, thus resulting in a best-fit period of 12. We limit rotation periods to <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub> < 12 days to avoid periodic earthshine signals at the beginning or end of each orbit in a given sector (B) TIC 408017296. Period of <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub> < 12 days was measured, but the width of the power peak is greater than expected and there is no noticeable periodic variability in the light curve. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure></div><h3 id="ajabac0as3-4" name="ajabac0as3-4">3.4. Identifying Flares</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The data used to train and validate the CNN required the flare to be at the center of each example. To predict where flares occur in other light curves, we used the CNN as a sliding box (with a baseline of 200 cadences) detector where each cadence is centered within the new examples, similar to the methods of Pearson et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib82" id="fnref-ajabac0abib82">2018</a>). This removed biases for finding flares that may or may not have occurred in the center of an example if we evenly divided the light curve into 200 cadences. As flares appear toward the center of the sliding box, the probability assigned to that cadence increases, as seen in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af12">12</a>. Each light curve was fed into the 10 <tt>stella</tt> models described in Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as2-4">2.4</a>. The output predictions from each model were averaged per light curve and used for flare identification.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af12" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af12" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af12_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 12."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 12. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>We considered every point in the “probability” light curve above a threshold of 0.5 to be a potential flare. Consecutive cadences of greater than the threshold were considered to be part of the same flare. The amplitude of the flare is defined as the point in the series with either the highest probability or, if several cadences share the same probability, the corresponding maximum normalized flux. Examples of identified flares can be seen in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af12">12</a>, where cadences are colored by the averaged probability identified with our ten CNN models. Both light curves were fed into the CNN as is. As the CNN requires 200 sequential cadences, without data gaps, the first and last 200 cadences of each orbit are ignored (Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af12">12</a>, “large” regions, orange points).</p><p>For each flare, we extract parameters by computing a <em>χ</em><sup>2 </sup>fit to an empirical flare model (Walkowicz et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib105" id="fnref-ajabac0abib105">2011</a>; Davenport et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib22" id="fnref-ajabac0abib22">2014</a>). We chose to model the flares with a sharp Gaussian rise and an exponential decay. The localized underlying stellar variability was removed before fitting the flare model by linearly interpolating across 100 cadences before and after the flare, where the flare itself is masked, and dividing this model from the light curve. Although flares sometimes show more complex structure, we found this simple model to result in reasonable fits to the flare amplitudes.</p><p>The CNN provides a good initial guess for where flares are located. However, due to a lack of completeness for flares down to low energies in the training set, we include minor additional checks that the event was a potential flare. Such checks include: (1) the amplitude of the flare must be 1.5<em>σ</em> ≥ the locally detrended light curve; (2) the two cadences directly following the amplitude must be 1<em>σ</em> ≥ the detrended light curve (i.e., at least three consecutive outlier points are considered part of a flare); (3) the cadence before and after the flare amplitude must be less than the amplitude; and (4) the amplitude must be ≥0.5%.</p></div></div><h2 class="header-anchor" id="ajabac0as4" name="ajabac0as4"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left fa-icon--flip" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 320 512"><path d="M137.4 374.6c12.5 12.5 32.8 12.5 45.3 0l128-128c9.2-9.2 11.9-22.9 6.9-34.9s-16.6-19.8-29.6-19.8L32 192c-12.9 0-24.6 7.8-29.6 19.8s-2.2 25.7 6.9 34.9l128 128z"></path></svg>4. Results</h2><div class="article-text" data-mobile-collapse=""><p>In total, we identified 17,479 flares across the 3193 stars in our sample. Of these, 14,618 had amplitudes <5% in the TESS bandpass. Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af11">11</a> shows Gaia color plotted against <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub> colored by age (top), maximum flare energy (middle), and flare rate (bottom). There is a noticeable decrease in flare rate at Gaia <em>B</em><sub><em>p</em>
            </sub> − <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>
            </sub> < 2, where <em>B</em><sub><em>p</em>
            </sub> − <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>
            </sub> = 2 corresponds to <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≈4000 K. For Sun-like stars and hotter, there is a clear drop-off in flare energies, with many stars not experiencing any flares and thus being absent from the middle plot. Notsu et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib75" id="fnref-ajabac0abib75">2019</a>) found a decrease in maximum flare energy with increasing rotation period for Kepler stars. Additionally, Tu et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib100" id="fnref-ajabac0abib100">2020</a>) observed the maximum flare energy as a function of rotation period for Solar-like stars in TESS data and found similar results. Magnetic activity is heightened for shorter rotation periods; it is interesting to note that we find no such relationship here with regard to the maximum flare energy as a function of rotation period. All young stars of the same color show similar flare energies across rotation periods.</p><h3 id="ajabac0as4-1" name="ajabac0as4-1">4.1. Flare Rates as a Function of Age and Temperature</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The flare rates are evaluated as a function of both stellar effective temperature and age. Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af13">13</a> is binned by flare energy and colored by ages <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> ≤ 50 Myr (black) and <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> > 50 Myr (blue); each subplot represents different spectral types. All flare analysis was weighted by the probability assigned by the CNN, as a flare with a 50% probability has an equal chance of being a flare or a non-flare. This figure is additionally binned in log-space and features a range of energies from 10<sup>29</sup>–10<sup>35</sup> erg. The coolest stars exhibit greater flare rates across all energies and many more low-energy flares, with a tail extending out to 10<sup>35</sup> ergs. There is a detection bias against low-energy flares with increasing <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub>; the amplitudes of low-energy flares are smaller on hotter stars—and therefore are undetectable. Our minimum flare amplitude is 0.5%, which has an equivalent duration (ED), or area under the flare light curve, ∼1.5 s. For each temperature bin, we calculated the corresponding energy to such a flare. We found a relation of <em>E</em><sub>flare,min</sub> = 0.01 <span xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="inline-eqn"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aieqn6.gif" style="max-width: 100%;" alt="${T}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{8.65\pm 1.61}$" align="top" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex">{T}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{8.65\pm 1.61}</script></span></span>.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af13" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af13" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af13_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 13."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 13. Gray shaded region corresponds to the energies at which we expect to be able to detect flares on all stars in that subpanel. Flares are weighted by their assigned probability from the CNN. Temperature ranges are labeled in each subplot. There is a noticeable drop-off in flare rate and energy as the star’s temperature increases. M and late K dwarfs (2300 ≤ <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 4000 K) experience similar flare rates and energy across the entire range of our sample. We do not recover any flares on stars 6200 ≤ <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 15,000 K older than 50 Myr.</p></div><p class="mb-05 print-hide">Download figure:</p><span class="btn-multi-block print-hide"><a class="btn btn-primary fig-dwnld-std-img" id="wd-jnl-art-btn-std-img-ajabac0af13" aria-labelledby="wd-jnl-art-btn-std-img-ajabac0af13 ajabac0af13-label" href="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af13_lr.jpg"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M0 96C0 60.7 28.7 32 64 32H448c35.3 0 64 28.7 64 64V416c0 35.3-28.7 64-64 64H64c-35.3 0-64-28.7-64-64V96zM323.8 202.5c-4.5-6.6-11.9-10.5-19.8-10.5s-15.4 3.9-19.8 10.5l-87 127.6L170.7 297c-4.6-5.7-11.5-9-18.7-9s-14.2 3.3-18.7 9l-64 80c-5.8 7.2-6.9 17.1-2.9 25.4s12.4 13.6 21.6 13.6h96 32H424c8.9 0 17.1-4.9 21.2-12.8s3.6-17.4-1.4-24.7l-120-176zM112 192a48 48 0 1 0 0-96 48 48 0 1 0 0 96z"></path></svg>Standard image

					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>The tail extends across all ages, with a more dominant presence in the ≤50 Myr stars. No flares were seen on <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≥ 6200 K and age <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> > 50 Myr. <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ∼ 6200 K roughly corresponds to the Kraft break (Heger et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib50" id="fnref-ajabac0abib50">2000</a>). Thus, a change in internal structure may be the cause of such a lack of flares, although we note our sample has very few stars in this bin. There are only 132 stars in this temperature range, and only three of these are older than 50 Myr.</p><p>Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af14">14</a> evaluates flare rates by temperature and binned in age ranges. We divided the sample at 4000 K because this corresponds to the steepest flare rate drop-off in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af11">11</a> (bottom panel). Across all age ranges, stars hotter than 4000 K (green) uniformly display smaller flare rates and amplitudes. The cooler stars have relatively consistent flare rates for both low- and high-energy flares in each age bin, demonstrating an overall level of heightened activity for these stars. There may be a slight increase in high-energy flares and flare rates between 1–20 Myr and 30–45 Myr stars cooler than 4000 K. This may be due to the fact that low-mass stars evolve more slowly onto the main sequence. These results are similar to those presented in Ilin et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib53" id="fnref-ajabac0abib53">2019</a>). However, the ages explored in this sample are much younger than theirs.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af14" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af14" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af14_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 14."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 14. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>In addition, we combined the subplots of Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af14">14</a> into flare frequency distributions (FFD) for <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 4000 K and <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> > 4000 K. A power law was fit to each FFD, with the same bin sizes. The slope of each was found to be <em>α</em><sub> ≤ 4000</sub> = −1.59 ± 0.03 and <em>α</em><sub> > 4000</sub> = −1.57 ± 0.04, which are within a 1.5<em>σ</em> agreement between the samples. We repeated the same calculation, but instead by fitting the FFD for <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> ≤ 50 Myr and <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> > 50 Myr. We find the slope of each to be <em>α</em><sub>≤50 Myr</sub> = −1.58 ± 0.03 and <em>α</em><sub>>50 Myr</sub> = −1.52 ± 0.08. The FFDs binned by age are likely dominated by the flare rate of the coolest stars. With TESS’s extended mission, more data on the same and different young stars may reveal a more significant difference in FFD slope as a function of temperature and age.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as4-2" name="ajabac0as4-2">4.2. Correlation between Spots and Flares</h3><div class="article-text"><p>The phase of the light curve was then mapped using the best-fit or averaged (if observed in multiple sectors) rotation period. One full rotation period has a range of phases: −0.5 <<em>ϕ</em> < 0.5, where the peak of the spot modulation is at <em>ϕ</em> = 0. The phase was mapped at each orbit. Partial rotations near the beginning/end or orbit gap were extrapolated from the surrounding full rotation periods.</p><p>Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af15">15</a> shows a histogram of flares with respect to phase, where the <em>ϕ</em> bin sizes are 0.04. Low (<5%, purple) and high (≥5%, yellow) amplitude flares are separated. For both samples, there is a consistent spread in number of flares at each phase. These results are broadly consistent with those of Notsu et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib76" id="fnref-ajabac0abib76">2013</a>) and Doyle et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib31" id="fnref-ajabac0abib31">2018</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib30" id="fnref-ajabac0abib30">2019</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib29" id="fnref-ajabac0abib29">2020</a>). These previous studies looked at flare rates versus phase for samples of size ∼100–200, while here we find the same effect with a sample size of 1500. Taken together, we interpret Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af15">15</a> as evidence for a magnetic active region coverage that is large and mostly uniformly distributed in longitude.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af15" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af15" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af15_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 15."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 15. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>Starspots are dark regions on a star originating from a concentration of magnetic field lines in the photosphere. As such, it is believed that flares will likely occur near these concentrations, as seen on the Sun (Dun et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib32" id="fnref-ajabac0abib32">2007</a>; Zhang et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib106" id="fnref-ajabac0abib106">2008</a>). By fitting a sine-wave to the overall sample of flares presented in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af15">15</a> at the same phase as the <em>x</em>-axis, we find a 3% difference in the flares between <em>ϕ</em> = 0 and <em>ϕ</em> = ±0.5. This small phase dependence means that the projected filling factor of stellar active regions remains relatively constant as seen from our viewing location. The on-average 2% spot-induced variability seen in the TESS light curves must be the result of stars covered in starspots, with only slight differences between the most and least spotted projected hemispheres. In the TESS bandpass (600–1000 nm), the Sun would be observed to have part-per-thousand variability. The surfaces of the stars in our sample would be very different compared to the Sun. Stellar active regions on this sample of young stars exhibit a large coverage fraction, with a large degree of longitudinal symmetry. Such symmetries can arise from potentially a few large spots, very many small spots, circumpolar or polar spots on inclined stars, or active latitudes peppered with spots (Guo et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib46" id="fnref-ajabac0abib46">2018</a>; Rackham et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib87" id="fnref-ajabac0abib87">2018</a>). The latitudinal distribution of starspots as a function of age is generally unknown, with evidence for circumpolar starspots on both young and evolved stars (Donati & Landstreet <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib27" id="fnref-ajabac0abib27">2009</a>; Roettenbacher et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib89" id="fnref-ajabac0abib89">2016</a>). Such high-latitude structures may act to mask the mapping from light-curve amplitude to total starspot coverage (Guo et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib46" id="fnref-ajabac0abib46">2018</a>) as spots remain in view on moderately inclined stars. Such viewing angle effects could explain the relatively uniform frequency of flares with rotational phase.</p><p>GJ 1243 is a known older active M dwarf that Hawley et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib47" id="fnref-ajabac0abib47">2014</a>) found to have no correlation between starspots and flares. That paper proposed two explanations: there is either significant spot coverage or a large polar spot consistently in the field of view. While polar spots would have different effects as a function of inclination, the effects of high spot coverage would look broadly similar across a large sample of stars. As our sample contains a large selection of stars likely at a variety of inclinations, and we see no significant correlations across our sample, our results favor the high spot coverage scenario for GJ 1243 and other active systems.</p><p>Nearly 10 yr of observations of the T Tauri star V410 Tau concluded in a relative coverage from 29%–41% coverage on the less spotted hemisphere to 61%–67% on the more spotted hemisphere (Grankin <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib42" id="fnref-ajabac0abib42">1999</a>). LkCa 4 was found to have a total starspot coverage fraction of 74%–86% on LkCa 4, for an asymmetric-to-total spot coverage ratio of 15% (Gully-Santiago et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib43" id="fnref-ajabac0abib43">2017</a>). Detailed studies of low-mass members of the Pleiades (∼112 Myr) suggest ∼30% and ∼50% spot coverage may be common for young M and K dwarfs, respectively (Stauffer et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib98" id="fnref-ajabac0abib98">2003</a>; Fang et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib34" id="fnref-ajabac0abib34">2016</a>). With such varying differences of spot coverage star to star, but with consistency in significant coverage up to 112 Myr, detailed studies of each star with spot modulation would need to be completed to truly understand the underlying distribution of spots.</p><p>However, understanding the coverage fraction of spots does not provide insight into the shape and nature of the spots. Rackham et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib87" id="fnref-ajabac0abib87">2018</a>) modeled light curves with varying spot coverage levels with both small (Sun-like, <em>R</em><sub>spot</sub> = 2°) and large (<em>R</em><sub>spot</sub> = 7°) spots. For the similar level of spot coverage, the large spots resulted in spot variability amplitudes greater than those of the small spots. They also concluded the relationship between spot coverage and observed variability is nonlinear.</p><p>Morris (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib70" id="fnref-ajabac0abib70">2020</a>) estimated the spot coverage of 531 F-K type stars across 10 Myr–4 Gyr, finding spot coverage decreases exponentially as ∝<em>t</em><sup>−0.37</sup>, where <em>t</em> is stellar age given in Gyr. For the sample presented here, this would suggest a spot coverage of 1%–13% for the oldest to youngest stars. Even when broken down by age, Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af15">15</a> remains relatively constant across phase. This suggests that, even at older ages, the total spot coverage fraction must be very large and may be underestimated from methods based on light curves; those methods are largely only sensitive to hemispherical asymmetries and rely heavily on uncertain geometrical assumptions on the longitudinal spot distribution.</p></div></div><h2 class="header-anchor" id="ajabac0as5" name="ajabac0as5"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left fa-icon--flip" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 320 512"><path d="M137.4 374.6c12.5 12.5 32.8 12.5 45.3 0l128-128c9.2-9.2 11.9-22.9 6.9-34.9s-16.6-19.8-29.6-19.8L32 192c-12.9 0-24.6 7.8-29.6 19.8s-2.2 25.7 6.9 34.9l128 128z"></path></svg>5. Discussion</h2><div class="article-text" data-mobile-collapse=""><h3 id="ajabac0as5-1" name="ajabac0as5-1">5.1. Comparing to Previous Flare Identification Methods</h3><div class="article-text"><p>We completed an injection-recovery test to compare the results of the CNN to previous methods. <tt>stella</tt> was trained on real flare events; injected flares do not perfectly model such events. Therefore, we do not expect the performance of <tt>stella</tt> on this sample to be identical to the performance on real data, and the results of this test should be viewed as an imperfect estimate of the effectiveness of the predictive model. The results of this test thus do not provide a definite result of how well <tt>stella</tt> is doing compared to previous methods. In order to completely quantify the differences, a more detailed study would need to be completed, which is beyond the scope of this analysis.</p><p>The injected flare amplitudes were randomly chosen from a normal distribution centered around a 4% flux increase from the baseline light curve. Ten flares were injected in 2263 of the light curves, those with measured rotation periods, in our sample. The injected light curves were then processed using the <tt>stella</tt> CNN and flare identification module. To compare to previous methods, we chose to follow the methods of Chang et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib16" id="fnref-ajabac0abib16">2015</a>) (Equations (3)(a)–(d)), which have been used for flare analyses for both Kepler and K2 data (Davenport <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib20" id="fnref-ajabac0abib20">2016</a>; Ilin et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib53" id="fnref-ajabac0abib53">2019</a>). We used a Savitsky-Golay filter of window length = 15 (Davenport <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib20" id="fnref-ajabac0abib20">2016</a>), as implemented in <tt>lightkurve</tt>, to detrend the spot modulation in the light curves before applying the flare heuristics. An aggressively small kernel size was used to combat the range of rotation periods measured in the sample.</p><p>We used a probability threshold of 0.5 for positively identified flares with <tt>stella</tt>. The injected flares may not perfectly represent the real astrophysics behind a flare, which the CNN was originally trained on. As such, an injection recovery provides useful guidance for comparison between methods, but should <em>not</em> be interpreted as a definitive efficacy. Nevertheless, the injected flares can provide some insight into overall trends in flare detection. While both methods recover all flares of amplitudes greater than 11% flux increase, there is a steep drop-off in recovered low-amplitude and generally lower-energy flares for previous methods. The CNN is able to recover 80% of injected flares below 5% flux increase. The resulting distribution of recovered flares with <tt>stella</tt> is similar to the injected sample, while previous methods are more centered at higher flare amplitudes and do not accurately represent the underlying distribution of injected flares.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as5-2" name="ajabac0as5-2">5.2. Largest Discovered Flares</h3><div class="article-text"><p>A selected sample of some of the highest amplitude flares recovered in this work are shown in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af16">16</a>. The light curves have been normalized and are labeled by the best age estimation for that star. The best-fit young population membership and stellar parameters are presented in the figure caption. There is clear underlying spot modulation for most of the stars plotted (left column), and the superflare is highlighted with a different <em>y</em>-scale limit to the right. These four stars span a temperature range of <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> = 2800 − 3200 K and luminosity values between 0.001 − 0.02<em>L</em><sub>⊙</sub>, as provided in the TIC, and are representative of all stars with flares amplitudes ≥100%.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af16" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af16" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af16_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 16."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 16. 					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>The ED and the luminosity can be combined to estimate flare energy in the TESS band. We use the simple flare model described previously to estimate the ED. Note that the flare models used are a rough estimate. Large flares are sometimes found to be followed by lower-energy sympathetic flares, which extend the exponential decay (Davenport et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib22" id="fnref-ajabac0abib22">2014</a>). The models used to estimate the ED and energy of these flares do not include this potential feature.</p><p>The resulting flare energies, in ascending age order for the targets displayed in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af16">16</a> (TIC 24721262, TIC 77954300, TIC 206544316, and TIC 44678751), are: 3 × 10<sup>35</sup>, 1 × 10<sup>37</sup>, 7 × 10<sup>36</sup>, and 2 × 10<sup>37</sup> erg. The “Carrington” superflare event on the Sun in 1859 released ∼10<sup>32</sup> erg, which is several orders of magnitude weaker than the strongest flares found in this work (Carrington <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib15" id="fnref-ajabac0abib15">1859</a>; Hodgson <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib51" id="fnref-ajabac0abib51">1859</a>). Using the <em>V, J, H</em> magnitude relation in Stassun et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib97" id="fnref-ajabac0abib97">2017</a>) along with the measured flare amplitude, we find the change in magnitude for these stars during the flares to be Δ<em>V</em> = 3.22, 4.11, 3.52, and 4.21 for the latter three targets. Flares are treated as a 9000 K blackbody (Kretzschmar <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib60" id="fnref-ajabac0abib60">2011</a>). As there was no V magnitude available for TIC 24721262, we used the G magnitude as an estimation.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as5-3" name="ajabac0as5-3">5.3. Repercussions for Exoplanets</h3><div class="article-text"><p>As the confirmed number of low-mass stars hosting exoplanets increases (e.g., Gillon et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib40" id="fnref-ajabac0abib40">2017</a>; Luger et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib66" id="fnref-ajabac0abib66">2017</a>; Feinstein et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib36" id="fnref-ajabac0abib36">2019b</a>; Günther et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib44" id="fnref-ajabac0abib44">2019</a>; Kostov et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib59" id="fnref-ajabac0abib59">2019</a>), so too does the need to understand the environment in which these planets grow and reside. High flare rates and high-energy radiation of main-sequence stars have raised questions about the habitability of these planets. It could inhibit the evolution of life through the suppression or destruction of an atmosphere (Tilley et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib99" id="fnref-ajabac0abib99">2019</a>). Alternatively, flares could create prebiotic molecules to ignite the complex chemistry required for life and allow for increased greenhouse warming (Airapetian et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib3" id="fnref-ajabac0abib3">2016</a>).</p><p>Both the frequency and energy of the flares can affect exoplanet atmospheres. Simulations of the flares from AD Leo, an active M dwarf, on two different modeled planets found that a single high-energy flare (<em>E</em> ∼ 10<sup>34</sup> erg; Hawley & Pettersen <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib48" id="fnref-ajabac0abib48">1991</a>) was sufficient to irreversibly alter the chemical composition of the atmospheres (Venot et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib102" id="fnref-ajabac0abib102">2016</a>). Specifically, the relative abundances of hydrogen, ammonia, carbon dioxide, nitric oxide, and hydroxide as a function of atmospheric pressure were significantly different ∼30,000 yr after a flare was injected, leading to the conclusion that planets around very active stars are constantly and permanently altered by these events. The highest-amplitude flares in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af16">16</a> are 1–3 orders of magnitude larger than the flare for AD Leo. Although Segura et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib93" id="fnref-ajabac0abib93">2010</a>) found the enhanced UV radiation did not affect the habitability of an Earth-like planet around AD Leo, they did not account for short-duration, high-energy flares. Vida et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib103" id="fnref-ajabac0abib103">2017</a>) analyzed the flares produced by TRAPPIST-1 in the available K2 light curve and concluded that both the high frequency and energies are likely disadvantageous for life.</p><p>Only a handful of transiting exoplanets around young stars are known, e.g., K2-25, K2-33, DS Tuc Ab, and V1298 Tau bcde (David et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib24" id="fnref-ajabac0abib24">2016</a>; Mann et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib68" id="fnref-ajabac0abib68">2016</a>; Benatti et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib9" id="fnref-ajabac0abib9">2019</a>; David et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib25" id="fnref-ajabac0abib25">2019b</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib23" id="fnref-ajabac0abib23">2019a</a>; Newton et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib73" id="fnref-ajabac0abib73">2019</a>). The atmospheres of these planets are believed to be highly extended and rapidly evolving. The “radius gap” in Kepler planets at ∼1.6<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub> has been theorized to be the result of significant photoevaporation of atmospheres within the first 100 Myr (Owen & Wu <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>). The models from (Owen & Wu <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>) considered a higher background UV environment for the exoplanet atmospheres, but did not include flares. The results presented here suggest high flare rates and amplitudes within the first 125 Myr for stars <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> > 4000  K. Cooler stars demonstrate high rates across 800 Myr.</p><p>We combined the methods described in Owen & Wu (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>) and Owen & Campos Estrada (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib78" id="fnref-ajabac0abib78">2020</a>) to study the evolution of atmospheric mass of an exoplanet over time. Additionally, the equations were modified to account for “flare-like” events, or short bursts of high-energy luminosity. We evaluated the potential impact of flares on V1298 Tau d, a 23 Myr old 6.41<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub> planet at <em>a</em> = 0.108 au separation discovered with K2 (David et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib25" id="fnref-ajabac0abib25">2019b</a>). The following additional assumptions about the planet were made: (1) the iron fraction in the core, <em>X</em><sub>iron</sub> = 1/3; (2) the ice fraction in the core, <em>X</em><sub>ice</sub> = 0; (3) the mass of the core, <em>M</em><sub>core</sub> = 5<em>M</em><sub>⊕</sub>; (4) the mass-loss efficiency, <em>η</em> = 0.2. The mass-loss rate due to photoevaporation is then given by</p><div xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="display-eqn" id="ajabac0aeqn1"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" style="max-width: 100%;" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aeqn1.gif" alt="Equation (1)" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex; mode=display">\begin{eqnarray}&&\dot{M}=\eta \displaystyle \frac{\pi {R}_{p}^{3}{L}_{\mathrm{HE}}}{4\pi {a}^{2}{{GM}}_{\mathrm{core}}}f(A),\end{eqnarray}
				\tag{
				1
				}
			</script></span></div><p>where <em>L</em><sub>HE</sub> is the luminosity of high-energy photons from the star, <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>
               </sub> is the radius of the planet, <em>a</em> is the semimajor axis (Owen & Wu <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>), and <em>f</em>(<em>A</em>) is a factor of mass-loss rate increase as a function of flare amplitude, <em>A</em>. This factor in the presence of a flare follows the relations found in Bisikalo et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib11" id="fnref-ajabac0abib11">2018</a>), and takes the form of <em>f</em>(<em>A</em>) = 0.95<em>A</em><sup>2.6</sup>. We assumed an <em>L</em><sub><em>HE</em>
               </sub> following Equation 22 in Owen & Wu (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>), which remains constant for the first 100 Myr and decays afterward as <span xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="inline-eqn"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aieqn7.gif" style="max-width: 100%;" alt="${{\rm{t}}}_{\mathrm{age}}^{-1.5}$" align="top" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex">{{\rm{t}}}_{\mathrm{age}}^{-1.5}</script></span></span>. Although several studies have shown a correlation between flare rate and <em>L</em><sub><em>HE</em>
               </sub> (Maehara et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib67" id="fnref-ajabac0abib67">2017</a>; Notsu et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib75" id="fnref-ajabac0abib75">2019</a>), these were for solar-type stars and may not apply to young K dwarfs like V1298 Tau. Flare amplitudes were injected up to 100× the base luminosity as observed in the TESS bandpass. We include an additional parameter, <em>s</em>, which converts the observed flare amplitudes in TESS to the amplitude observed in broad UV wavelength range, and was calculated by</p><div xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="display-eqn" id="ajabac0aeqn2"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" style="max-width: 100%;" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aeqn2.gif" alt="Equation (2)" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex; mode=display">\begin{eqnarray}&&s={\int }_{\mathrm{TESS}}\displaystyle \frac{{B}_{\lambda }({T}_{\mathrm{eff}})}{{B}_{\lambda }({T}_{\mathrm{flare}})}d\lambda {\left[{\int }_{\mathrm{UV}}\displaystyle \frac{{B}_{\lambda }({T}_{\mathrm{eff}})}{{B}_{\lambda }({T}_{\mathrm{flare}})}d\lambda \right]}^{-1},\end{eqnarray}
				\tag{
				2
				}
			</script></span></div><p>where <em>B</em><sub><em>λ</em>
               </sub>(<em>T</em>) is the Planck function, the TESS bandpass covers 600–1000 nm, and the UV covers 66–365 nm. We have assumed all flares can be represented as a 9000 K blackbody (Kretzschmar <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib60" id="fnref-ajabac0abib60">2011</a>). For V1298 Tau, where <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> = 4970 K (David et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib23" id="fnref-ajabac0abib23">2019a</a>), <em>s</em> = 14.6, which indicates flares would appear 14.6× brighter if observed in the UV. At each time step, there was a ∼33% chance of a flare being injected, which is a probability similar to that of observing a flare in the TESS light curves.</p><p>The evolution of the atmospheric mass as a function of time is shown in Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af17">17</a> for three different scenarios: one with no flares (purple, following the original methods of Owen & Wu (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib79" id="fnref-ajabac0abib79">2017</a>) and Owen & Campos Estrada (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib78" id="fnref-ajabac0abib78">2020</a>)), one with flares present for the first 200 Myr (blue), and the third with flares present throughout 1000 Myr (green). The injection of flares does show an effect on the final atmosphere mass. In the case of flares present for the first 200 Myr, the planet loses 4% more atmosphere than without flares. For the case of flares persistent across 1000 Myr, the planet loses 7% more atmosphere. Because the only parameter changing between models is <em>f</em>(<em>A</em>) and we are evaluating ratios, the composition assumptions above listed do not have an effect on these values.</p><figure xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="ajabac0af17" tabindex="-1" role="group" class="boxout boxout-bdr-grey keyboard-focus-only" data-toolbar-type="figure" data-toolbar-link="ajabac0af17" data-toolbar-img="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af17_lr.jpg" data-toolbar-title="Figure 17."><figure><div class="panzoom-container"><div class="panzoom-parent" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;"><img class="panzoom" alt="Figure 17.
