Purple lines correspond to a high-energy luminosity without flares; blue corresponds to flares being present in the first 200 Myr; green corresponds to flares being present throughout all the 1000 Myr. Presence of flares affects the atmosphere mass, with flares present over a longer period of time removing more mass.</p></div><p class="mb-05 print-hide">Download figure:</p><span class="btn-multi-block print-hide"><a class="btn btn-primary fig-dwnld-std-img" id="wd-jnl-art-btn-std-img-ajabac0af17" aria-labelledby="wd-jnl-art-btn-std-img-ajabac0af17 ajabac0af17-label" href="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af17_lr.jpg"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M0 96C0 60.7 28.7 32 64 32H448c35.3 0 64 28.7 64 64V416c0 35.3-28.7 64-64 64H64c-35.3 0-64-28.7-64-64V96zM323.8 202.5c-4.5-6.6-11.9-10.5-19.8-10.5s-15.4 3.9-19.8 10.5l-87 127.6L170.7 297c-4.6-5.7-11.5-9-18.7-9s-14.2 3.3-18.7 9l-64 80c-5.8 7.2-6.9 17.1-2.9 25.4s12.4 13.6 21.6 13.6h96 32H424c8.9 0 17.1-4.9 21.2-12.8s3.6-17.4-1.4-24.7l-120-176zM112 192a48 48 0 1 0 0-96 48 48 0 1 0 0 96z"></path></svg>Standard image
					</a><a class="btn btn-primary fig-dwnld-hi-img" id="wd-jnl-art-btn-hires-img-ajabac0af17" aria-labelledby="wd-jnl-art-btn-hires-img-ajabac0af17 ajabac0af17-label" href="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0af17_hr.jpg"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 512 512"><path d="M0 96C0 60.7 28.7 32 64 32H448c35.3 0 64 28.7 64 64V416c0 35.3-28.7 64-64 64H64c-35.3 0-64-28.7-64-64V96zM323.8 202.5c-4.5-6.6-11.9-10.5-19.8-10.5s-15.4 3.9-19.8 10.5l-87 127.6L170.7 297c-4.6-5.7-11.5-9-18.7-9s-14.2 3.3-18.7 9l-64 80c-5.8 7.2-6.9 17.1-2.9 25.4s12.4 13.6 21.6 13.6h96 32H424c8.9 0 17.1-4.9 21.2-12.8s3.6-17.4-1.4-24.7l-120-176zM112 192a48 48 0 1 0 0-96 48 48 0 1 0 0 96z"></path></svg>High-resolution image
					</a></span></figcaption></figure></figure><p>As the mass-loss rate is linearly proportional the high-energy luminosity (<span xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="inline-eqn"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aieqn8.gif" style="max-width: 100%;" alt="$\dot{M}\propto f(A)$" align="top" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex">\dot{M}\propto f(A)</script></span></span>), we would expect the mass loss to increase with respect to flare amplitude. Therefore, stars that have flares that are 40–60× the base flux (e.g., Paudel et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib80" id="fnref-ajabac0abib80">2018</a>, <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib81" id="fnref-ajabac0abib81">2019</a>) will increase the mass loss proportionally, thus resulting in even smaller fractional retention of the atmospheric mass. Additionally, the radius of the planet changes due to atmospheric loss changes, originally starting at <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>
               </sub> = 6.41<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub> and predicted to evolve to <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>, none</sub> = 2.11<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub>. With the inclusion of flares, we find the final evolved radius to be <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>,200</sub> = 2.10<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub> and <em>R</em><sub><em>p</em>,1000</sub> = 2.09<em>R</em><sub>⊕</sub> for each model. Although these radius changes are smaller than the typical uncertainties in planet radii, these are physical changes brought about when including flares in atmospheric photoevaporation modeling.</p><p>The magnetic field of the planet should also be accounted for. Kay et al. (<a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib56" id="fnref-ajabac0abib56">2016</a>) explored the impacts of M dwarf coronal-mass ejections, sometimes associated with flares, on exoplanets; they found that rocky exoplanets would need to generate magnetic field strengths of tens to hundreds of Gauss, much stronger than fields in the solar system, to protect its atmosphere against these events. The presence of a magnetosphere will directly affect the amount of energy from the flare that reaches the atmosphere, which then directly affects the mass-loss efficiency, <em>η</em>. Future analyses should consider flares when thinking about mass-loss efficiencies.</p></div><h3 id="ajabac0as5-4" name="ajabac0as5-4">5.4. Limitations and Future Work</h3><div class="article-text"><p>Due to random alignments of stars with respect to our line of sight, one may expect a handful of stars without measured <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub> that exhibit flare rates similar to those with measured <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub>. These could be the result of either highly longitudinally symmetric spot distributions or a nearly pole-on stellar inclination, where polar starspots are consistently observed and thus show no obvious spot modulation. Additional follow-up of our sample with <span xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" class="inline-eqn"><span class="tex"><span class="texImage"><img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=" data-src="https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/1538-3881/160/5/219/revision3/ajabac0aieqn9.gif" style="max-width: 100%;" alt="$v\sin i$" align="top" role="math"></img></span><script type="math/tex">v\sin i</script></span></span> measurements could help to estimate the otherwise difficult-to-measure latitudinal distribution of starspots. The presence of high-latitude spots could explain the lack of flare phase dependence (Figure <a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" href="#ajabac0af15">15</a>), as polar spots are always visible. Sharp spectral lines in pole-on stars would make them amenable to direct measurement of starspot emission even for small coverage fractions of starspots, since high spectral resolution can perceive individual weak photospheric lines arising from collective starspot emission. Candidate pole-on stars in this sample would have to be reassessed to obtain <em>P</em><sub>rot</sub>, since the measurement criteria discussed in Section <a class="secref" href="#ajabac0as3-3">3.3</a> may have missed potentially weak rotation signatures.</p><p>There are a few instances where <tt>stella</tt> improperly characterizes a light-curve feature as a flare. First, these improper characterizations are mainly constrained to stars with measurable rotation periods of ≤0.5 days, contact binaries with sharp modulation features, and generally noisy light curves. This may be due to a limited sample of such stars in the original training set of the CNN. Second, the metric results of our CNN could be improved by resampling the training set to oversample the lowest-amplitude flares in each batch set. As such, we hope to improve the overall recovery rate of flares with <tt>stella</tt> by incorporating the new flare and non-flare examples identified in this work into the training, testing, and validation sets for future work. Third, users of <tt>stella</tt> who want the most complete flare-only catalog with minimal contamination from noise should explore using a higher threshold probability metric. If users want a small sample of high-fidelity flares, they should explore different threshold values to obtain the desired flare results. This metric can be set in the <tt>stella</tt> code and will not affect the included pre-trained models.</p><p>The methods explored in this work provide hope for studying other events around young active stars, such as searching for exoplanet transits. Although this sample used real flares as the training set for the CNN, transits can easily be modeled and injected into young stellar light curves. CNNs have been trained to find transits in K2 data (e.g., Pearson et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib82" id="fnref-ajabac0abib82">2018</a>), but these searches have not been tailored toward young stars in TESS. We believe a CNN architecture similar to that created here would work well for transits, and we plan to explore this question in the near future.</p><p>The light curves processed in this work as well as the CNN models created will be hosted as a high-level science product (HLSP) at the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). Additionally, <tt>stella</tt> is an open-source package that can be downloaded through GitHub or via the Python Package Index. <tt>stella</tt> includes the ability to create custom CNN model architectures, as well as all of the rotation measurements and flare fitting described in this work. As the models were trained on TESS two-minute data, users can predict flares in their own light curves of the same format with our models.<sup class="fnref"><a class="fnref" href="#ajabac0afn4">
                  14
               </a></sup>
               
            </p></div></div><h2 class="header-anchor" id="ajabac0as6" name="ajabac0as6"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" class="fa-icon fa-icon--left fa-icon--flip" role="img" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 320 512"><path d="M137.4 374.6c12.5 12.5 32.8 12.5 45.3 0l128-128c9.2-9.2 11.9-22.9 6.9-34.9s-16.6-19.8-29.6-19.8L32 192c-12.9 0-24.6 7.8-29.6 19.8s-2.2 25.7 6.9 34.9l128 128z"></path></svg>6. Conclusions</h2><div class="article-text" data-mobile-collapse=""><p>We have presented the use of a convolutional neural network to identify flares and understand flare rates across a range of young (<em>t</em><sub>age</sub> < 800 Myr) ages in TESS two-minute light curves. Our key findings are the following:</p><ol class="clear-list wd-inline-list" style="list-style-type: none;"><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">1.  </div><div class="indices-content">CNNs are a promising method for flare detection and are able to recover more flares at lower energies (<5% flare amplitude) than previously used light-curve detrending and sigma-outlier methods.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">2.  </div><div class="indices-content">There appears to be no preference for flare occurrence and spot phase across all flare energies. As flares and spots are both magnetically driven events, this may be used to infer that neither hemisphere is spot-free, but rather the variability is driven by a different spot coverage fraction.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">3.  </div><div class="indices-content">Low-mass stars (<em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> < 4000 K) show higher flare rates and larger flare energies across all ages of our sample. Hotter stars show higher flare rates and larger flare amplitudes at <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> ≤ 50 Myr, and they evolve to slower rates and weaker flares as they age. Stars with <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> = 6200–15,000 show no flares at any amplitude for ages <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> > 50 Myr.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">4.  </div><div class="indices-content">We find that, across all ages, stars with <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 4000 K exhibit higher flare rates and flare energies than hotter stars. There is a slight increase in flare rate for cool stars in age bins <em>t</em><sub>age</sub> = 1–20 Myr to 45–125 Myr. Low-mass stars are believed to reach the zero age main sequence at 50 Myr (Zuckerman et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib109" id="fnref-ajabac0abib109">2004</a>). The peak of this flare rate in the 45–125 Myr bin may indicate the turn-on of these stars to the main sequence. However, a larger study of cool stars may be needed to further explore this relation.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">5.  </div><div class="indices-content">The largest flares were all found on late M dwarfs (<em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ≤ 3200 K). As the fully convective boundary is at <em>T</em><sub>eff</sub> ∼ 3300 K (Dorman et al. <a class="cite" href="#ajabac0abib28" id="fnref-ajabac0abib28">1989</a>), this suggests different internal processes driving the creation of such energetic flares.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">6.  </div><div class="indices-content">Modeled atmospheric mass loss due to photoevaporation suggests the inclusion of flares decreases the final atmospheric mass and planet radius when compared to models not accounting for flares. Thus, flares should be accounted for in such models moving forward.</div></li><li class="indices-list"><div class="indices-id">7.  </div><div class="indices-content">We hope to improve our CNN by incorporating our newly found flares and more examples of very fast (<0.5 days) rotators in the training, validation, and test sets. We also plan on testing this CNN architecture and sliding box method to find new transiting exoplanets around young stars.</div></li></ol><p>
